title: Prepositions
tagline: Grammar · time, place, movement and fixed word-preposition pairs

sourceNote.boardprep: All rules, tables, example sentences, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written for practice and are not taken from any textbook, guide or past paper.

overview.intro: A preposition shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence: where something is, when something happens, or how two things are connected. English has a small number of prepositions but a great many fixed pairings with verbs, adjectives and nouns, and these must be learnt. This chapter sets out the patterns for time and place, the difficult pairs and the mistakes students most often make.

facts.label: Main idea
facts.value: A preposition links a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence

facts.label: Time
facts.value: at for clock time, on for days and dates, in for months, years and long periods

facts.label: Place
facts.value: at for a point, in for an enclosed space, on for a surface

facts.label: Fixed pairs
facts.value: Many words take one particular preposition, such as fond of and depend on

facts.label: Watch
facts.value: Some verbs take no preposition: discuss, enter, reach, attend

blocks.text: A preposition is followed by a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form, which is called its object. If a pronoun follows a preposition it takes the object form: with him, for us, between you and me. Prepositions are short words but they change meaning completely: compare in the room, on the room and at the room, or a letter from him and a letter to him.

items.meaning: Exact times and points: at 9 a.m., at noon, at midnight, at night, at sunrise, at the weekend (British).
Days and dates: on Monday, on 15 August, on my birthday, on the first day.
Months, years, seasons, centuries and parts of the day: in July, in 2004, in winter, in the morning, in the evening. Also the time taken before something happens: The train will leave in ten minutes.
For gives the length of time (for two hours, for a week). Since gives the starting point (since Monday, since 2018).
By means not later than: Submit it by Friday. Until means up to that time: Wait until Friday.
During means throughout a period or at some point in it: during the holidays. Within means not more than: within a week.
A point or a place seen as a point: at the bus stop, at the door, at school, at the station.
Inside an enclosed area or a large area: in the room, in a box, in Delhi, in India.
On a surface or a line: on the table, on the wall, on the road, on the ceiling.

items.term: into, onto, out of, to, from
items.meaning: Movement: She walked into the hall. The cat jumped onto the shelf. He came out of the shop. We travelled from Pune to Mumbai.
Between is used for two (or for clear separate points): between the bank and the post office. Among is used for three or more, thought of as a group: The prize was shared among the winners.

Over and under are used for covering or direct contact and movement: a bridge over the river. Above and below are used for higher and lower levels: a picture above the desk; a temperature below zero. Beneath is a formal word for under.
Beside means next to: She sat beside me. Besides means in addition to: Besides English, he speaks Bengali.

learn.title: Fixed pairs: words and their prepositions

items.meaning: good at, weak in, fond of, afraid of, proud of, aware of, capable of, keen on, interested in, angry with a person, angry at a thing, jealous of, similar to, different from, superior to, inferior to, senior to, junior to, responsible for, famous for, full of, tired of, married to.

depend on, insist on, rely on, congratulate on, accuse of, suspect of, prevent from, differ from, suffer from, laugh at, look at, listen to, belong to, complain about, apologise to a person for a mistake, prefer one thing to another, agree with a person, agree to a proposal.
look forward to (followed by a noun or -ing form), in charge of, in spite of, on behalf of, because of, instead of, according to, in front of, by mistake, on purpose, at last.

discuss (not discuss about), enter (not enter into a room), reach (not reach to), attend (not attend to a class), marry (not marry with), request, resemble. Say: She discussed the plan. He entered the hall. We reached the station.

items.text: The meeting starts ___ 9 a.m. Answer: at.
She is very fond ___ classical music. Answer: of.
The prize was shared ___ the three winners. Answer: among.
items.note: Three or more, as a group.

items.text: He has been absent ___ Monday. Answer: since.
Rewrite with because of: The match was postponed since it rained heavily. Answer: The match was postponed because of heavy rain.
items.note: Because takes a clause; because of takes a noun phrase.

items.text: Rewrite with in spite of: Although it was raining, we played outside. Answer: In spite of the rain, we played outside.
items.note: Although takes a clause; in spite of takes a noun or an -ing form.

items.text: I prefer tea ___ coffee. Answer: to.
items.note: Prefer is followed by to, not than.

learn.title: Common mistakes and how to correct them

items.text: Wrong: He is good in mathematics. Right: He is good at mathematics.
items.note: Good at is the fixed pair.

items.text: Wrong: She entered into the hall. Right: She entered the hall.
Wrong: We discussed about the plan. Right: We discussed the plan.
Wrong: I am senior than him. Right: I am senior to him.
items.note: Senior, junior, superior and inferior take to.

items.text: Wrong: I prefer tea than coffee. Right: I prefer tea to coffee.
Wrong: She is angry on me. Right: She is angry with me.
items.note: With a person, angry with; at a thing, angry at.

items.text: Wrong: He has lived here from 2010. Right: He has lived here since 2010.
items.note: Present perfect needs since or for.

items.text: Wrong: I waited for him at two hours. Right: I waited for him for two hours.

items: Step 1. Look at the word just before the gap. If it is an adjective, verb or noun that has a fixed partner, use that partner.
Step 2. If the gap involves time, decide whether it is a point (at), a day or date (on), a longer period (in), a length (for) or a starting point (since).
Step 3. If the gap involves place, decide whether it is a point (at), an enclosed space (in) or a surface (on).
Step 4. Check the number of things: between for two, among for more than two.
Step 5. Check whether the verb needs a preposition at all: discuss, enter, reach and attend do not.
Step 6. Read the finished sentence and check that a pronoun after the preposition is in the object form.
Keep a personal list of fixed pairs and revise it in short bursts.

keyPoints: A preposition is followed by a noun, a pronoun in the object form, or an -ing form.
At is for exact times, on is for days and dates, in is for months, years, seasons and parts of the day.
Since names a starting point; for names a length of time.
At is for a point, in for an enclosed space and on for a surface.
Between is for two; among is for three or more.
Many words have fixed partners, such as good at, fond of, depend on and prefer to.
Discuss, enter, reach and attend take no preposition.
Beside means next to; besides means in addition to.
examFocus: Filling gaps with a suitable preposition.
Correcting a wrongly used preposition in a sentence.
Knowing fixed pairs of adjectives and verbs with prepositions.
Rewriting sentences using in spite of, because of, instead of and similar phrases.
Using since and for correctly with the right tense.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The meeting starts ___ 9 a.m. tomorrow.
questions.explanation: At is used with exact clock times.
questions.commonMistake: Using in or on with a clock time.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: She is very fond ___ classical music.
questions.commonMistake: Using for by analogy with keen on or eager for.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The prize was shared ___ the three winners.
questions.explanation: Among is used for three or more people or things thought of as a group.
questions.commonMistake: Using between for more than two.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: I prefer tea ___ coffee.
questions.explanation: The verb prefer is followed by to when two things are compared.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with a suitable preposition: The old man is suffering ___ a high fever.
questions.explanation: Suffer takes from when an illness is named.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with a suitable preposition: The school reopens ___ 3 July after the vacation.
questions.commonMistake: Using in because July is a month. The full date takes on.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with a suitable preposition: The bookshop stands ___ the bank and the post office.
questions.explanation: Two clearly separate points take between.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using 'in spite of': Although it was raining, we played outside.
questions.answer: In spite of the rain, we played outside.
questions.explanation: Although introduces a clause, whereas in spite of is followed by a noun phrase or an -ing form. In spite of the rain falling is also acceptable but less neat.
questions.commonMistake: Writing In spite of it was raining.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using 'because of': The match was postponed since it rained heavily.
questions.answer: The match was postponed because of heavy rain.
questions.explanation: Because of takes a noun phrase, so the clause it rained heavily becomes heavy rain.
questions.commonMistake: Writing because of it rained heavily.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference in use between the prepositions in, on and at when talking about place. Give one example of each.
questions.answer: In is used for an enclosed space or a large area: She is in the kitchen. On is used for a surface: The book is on the table. At is used for a point or a place thought of as a point: He is waiting at the bus stop.
questions.explanation: The answer should give the idea for each preposition and a correct example.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the three words are interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Each sentence has one error in the use of a preposition. Rewrite it correctly. (a) He is good in mathematics. (b) She entered into the hall. (c) We discussed about the plan. (d) I am senior than him.
questions.answer: (a) He is good at mathematics. (b) She entered the hall. (c) We discussed the plan. (d) I am senior to him.
questions.explanation: (a) Good at is the fixed pair. (b) and (c) The verbs enter and discuss take no preposition. (d) Senior, junior, superior and inferior take to.
questions.commonMistake: Changing the wrong word or replacing one wrong preposition with another wrong one.

questions.prompt: Complete each sentence with for or since: (a) She has lived here ___ ten years. (b) They have been friends ___ 2018. (c) We waited ___ a long time. (d) He has been ill ___ last winter.
questions.explanation: For is followed by a length of time (ten years, a long time). Since is followed by a starting point (2018, last winter).
questions.commonMistake: Choosing by the sound of the sentence instead of asking whether a length or a starting point follows.
